content: 1. A study by M. Aoyagi et al. in 2009 demonstrated that an early decline in hepatitis C virus (HCV) core antigen levels can predict sustained virologic response (SVR) in patients undergoing treatment with pegylated interferon and ribavirin combination therapy. This finding highlights the potential of HCV core antigen as a biomarker for treatment efficacy. 2. Research by Takahashi et al. in 2005 emphasized the utility of HCV core antigen assays in predicting therapeutic responses to interferon and ribavirin combination therapy. The study supports the role of core antigen testing as a valuable tool in clinical decision-making for HCV management. 3. A study by Fytyli et al. in 2007 investigated the frequency of very low HCV viremia using a highly sensitive HCV-RNA assay. The findings underscore the importance of advanced diagnostic tools in detecting low levels of viral RNA, which may have implications for disease monitoring and treatment strategies. 4. Diagnostic accuracy of HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) index tests for detecting active HCV infection was evaluated against nucleic acid testing (NAT) as the reference standard. Sensitivity and specificity results from various studies were reported, ranging from 8% to 100%, depending on the test type and study design. 5. The sensitivity and specificity of HCV core antigen assays in predicting SVR after initiating interferon-based treatment were analyzed. The results suggest that HCV core antigen testing can serve as a reliable predictor of treatment outcomes. 6. A systematic review identified 8146 potentially relevant citations from electronic databases, including PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus. After removing duplicates and screening, 50 studies were included in the final analysis. 7. The PRISMA diagrams provided detailed information on the inclusion and exclusion of studies for various research questions (PICO 5a, 5b, and 9). Reasons for exclusion included inappropriate reference standards, insufficient sample sizes, and lack of core antigen testing. 8. Forest plots and bivariate analyses were used to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of various HCV core antigen assays, including Abbott ARCHITECT, Ortho ELISA-Ag, Bio-Rad Monolisa, and Hunan Jynda ELISA. These analyses compared the performance of these assays to NAT, the gold standard for diagnosing active HCV infection. 9. The Abbott ARCHITECT HCV core antigen assay demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing active HCV infection, with pooled summary estimates and confidence intervals provided. The assay's performance was consistent across samples regardless of HCV antibody status. 10. The Ortho ELISA-Ag assay and Bio-Rad Monolisa HCV Ag-Ab ULTRA assay were also evaluated for their diagnostic accuracy. Both assays showed promising results in detecting active HCV infection when compared to NAT. 11. The analysis demonstrated a strong correlation, with a positivity threshold of 3 fmol/L for the core antigen index test. 12. The QUADAS-2 protocol was used to assess the risk of bias and applicability of included studies. Domains evaluated included patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow/timing. Most studies were judged to have a low risk of bias and high applicability to the review question. 13. The systematic review highlighted the importance of HCV core antigen testing as a diagnostic and monitoring tool for HCV infection. The findings support its use in clinical practice, particularly in settings where NAT may not be readily available. 14. The search strategies for databases such as Embase, Web of Knowledge, PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane were detailed, ensuring comprehensive coverage of relevant literature on HCV core antigen testing. 15. These tools facilitated the systematic evaluation of study design, population, and diagnostic accuracy. 16. The review concluded that HCV core antigen assays are effective for diagnosing active HCV infection and monitoring treatment response. However, variations in assay performance and study design highlight the need for standardized protocols and further research.
